past_medical_history: Migraine without aura in her thirties, long resolved
Sudden onset of confusion and drowsiness 8 months ago, admitted for 4 days, discharged with a diagnosis of 'transient confusional state'

medications.indication: Started after the admission 8 months ago

family_history: Mother had hypertension and died at 84
No family history of dementia or of early stroke

social_history.occupation: practising notary until 8 months ago, now on leave
social_history.living_situation: Lives with her husband; two adult children nearby

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. MoCA 23/30, but the score conceals the deficit: she loses all 5 points on delayed recall, recalling 0/5 unaided and only 1/5 with cueing and 2/5 on recognition. Verbal fluency 15 animals, trail-making completed, digit span backwards 1/1, serial sevens 5/5. She confabulates mildly when asked about the previous day and shows striking apathy and lack of concern about her own situation.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full without vertical gaze restriction. Visual fields full. Face symmetric. Speech fluent and articulate.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk, tone and strength throughout. No drift, no tremor.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal base, stride and arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.additional: Marked apathy with preserved social comportment. No frontal release signs. Pulse regular at 70.

patient.chief_complaint: Since a hospital admission eight months ago she cannot retain anything new and has not returned to work
patient.history_present_illness: Dr. Elena Marchetti is a 68-year-old notary who was admitted eight months ago with sudden confusion and drowsiness that developed over an hour while she was at her desk. She was hospitalised for four days, a CT of the head was reported as normal, and she was discharged on aspirin with a diagnosis of a transient confusional state. Her husband reports that she has never returned to her previous self. She is alert, articulate and socially appropriate — colleagues who meet her briefly notice nothing — but she cannot retain new information at all: she asks the same question repeatedly within the hour, cannot remember whether she has eaten, and has twice arranged two appointments for the same time. She has not been able to return to notarial work, where retention of case detail is essential. Strikingly, she is not distressed by any of this and does not spontaneously mention it; the account comes entirely from her husband. There has been no further abrupt event, no headache, no weakness, no visual symptoms, no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment. Her blood pressure has been in the 140-150 range. Her decline is not progressive: the deficit appeared on one day and has been stable since.

findings.location: Left anterior and paramedian thalamus, involving the mamillothalamic tract and the anterior nucleus

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: Well-defined hyperintense lesion with a cavitated centre in the left anteromedial thalamus

findings.type: White matter hyperintensity of presumed vascular origin

findings.location: None beyond the lesion; medial temporal lobes normal

signal_characteristics.Coronal_T1: Hippocampal formations symmetric and normal in volume

volumetrics.medial_temporal_atrophy: Scheltens MTA grade 0 — no hippocampal atrophy

additional_observations: The lesion involves the mamillothalamic tract and the anterior thalamic nucleus, interrupting the Papez circuit — the anatomical explanation for a dense anterograde amnesia produced by a 0.7 mL lesion
No restricted diffusion — the infarct is chronic and dates to the admission eight months ago
The head CT performed during that admission was reported as normal, which small thalamic infarcts commonly are
SWI shows no microbleeds; Fazekas 1 white matter change only
mri.impression: Chronic strategic infarct of the left anterior and paramedian thalamus involving the mamillothalamic tract, with a minimal small-vessel burden and no hippocampal atrophy. A 0.7 mL lesion in this location interrupts the anterior limb of the Papez circuit and accounts fully for a dense anterograde amnesia with apathy.

labs.interpretation: LDL 102 mg/dL is above target for a patient with a documented infarct. Thyroid function, B12, folate, RPR and HIV are normal or negative, excluding the reversible causes of an amnestic syndrome. There is no anaemia and renal function is normal.

advanced_imaging.tracer_or_protocol: Time-of-flight and contrast-enhanced MR angiography of the head and neck

findings.region: Basilar artery and posterior cerebral arteries

advanced_imaging.impression: No large-artery stenosis, occlusion or dissection. The thalamic infarct is attributable to occlusion of a small perforating artery, which is not amenable to revascularisation and is treated with risk-factor control.

quantitative_data.pattern: isolated amnestic syndrome of storage type
quantitative_data.recognition: impaired at the 2nd percentile, excluding a retrieval-only deficit

specialized_test.impression: A pure and severe anterograde amnesia: learning, free recall and recognition are all at or below the 2nd percentile while executive function, language and reasoning are at or above the population average. Impaired recognition places the deficit at the level of storage, which localises to the medial diencephalic memory circuit rather than to the frontal-subcortical networks affected by small-vessel disease.

findings.performance: 0/5 unaided, 1/5 cued, 2/5 recognition — dense, and not retrieval-type
Digit span backwards and serial sevens normal — spared
Apathy Evaluation Scale 52 — severe, with preserved social comportment

clinical_assessment.impression: MoCA 23/30 is misleading: attention, executive function, language and processing speed are all normal, and the entire loss falls on delayed recall, which is dense and does not benefit from cueing or recognition. This is a storage deficit with apathy and preserved comportment in a patient whose deficit appeared abruptly on one day — the profile of a strategic thalamic lesion, not of small-vessel disease.

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 9 Hz, symmetric, reactive to eye opening

eeg.impression: Normal awake EEG for age. No epileptiform discharges and no focal or generalised slowing.

labs.interpretation: The additional panels requested are negative and do not contribute to the diagnosis in this presentation.

findings.description: no finding relevant to this presentation

vascular_cognitive_impairment.query: vascular cognitive impairment diagnostic criteria and secondary prevention

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — strategic single-infarct type, left anterior and paramedian thalamic infarct interrupting the mamillothalamic tract

differential.key_features: The onset was abrupt on a documented day and the deficit has been stable for eight months rather than progressive; the hippocampi are normal at Scheltens 0 and executive function and language are above average
The deficit is continuous rather than episodic, there are no stereotyped attacks, and the thalamic infarct explains it
No alcohol history, no nutritional deficiency, no ophthalmoparesis or ataxia, and the lesion is unilateral thalamic rather than in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal grey
Fazekas 1 change and a normal executive profile exclude the diffuse subcortical mechanism; the deficit is focal
Recognition memory is impaired at the 2nd percentile with an anatomically coherent lesion; the pattern is not inconsistent or effort-dependent

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Abrupt onset on a single documented day eight months ago with a stable deficit since, dense anterograde amnesia with apathy and mild confabulation, and preserved social comportment — a step, not a progression

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 23/30 concealing a dense anterograde amnesia (0/5 unaided, 2/5 recognition) with normal attention, executive function and language, plus severe apathy — a focal profile disproportionate to the screen total

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes of an amnestic syndrome excluded; LDL above target for a patient with a documented infarct

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Chronic left anterior/paramedian thalamic infarct involving the mamillothalamic tract, 0.7 mL, with Fazekas 1 change and no hippocampal atrophy — a strategic lesion whose deficit is disproportionate to its volume

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Isolated severe anterograde amnesia of storage type with intact executive function, confirming a focal diencephalic lesion rather than a diffuse process

optimal_actions.action: Obtain MR angiography of the head and neck for intracranial large-artery stenosis or dissection
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patent artery of Percheron territory vessels with no stenosis or dissection; the infarct was small-vessel occlusion of a thalamic perforator, so no proximal lesion requires treatment

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Treat as secondary prevention after a documented infarct: intensify antihypertensive therapy toward a systolic below 130 mmHg, raise the statin to reach an LDL below 70 mg/dL, continue single antiplatelet therapy, and refer for memory rehabilitation with external aids plus an occupational assessment of her fitness to practise
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Secondary-prevention targets set, memory rehabilitation with external aids arranged, and the occupational question of fitness to practise formally addressed rather than left to her own judgement, which is impaired by the apathy

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Recognise that an abrupt onset on a single documented day with a stable deficit afterwards is a stroke syndrome, not a degenerative one
Look past the screening total: a MoCA of 23 with all points lost on one domain is a focal deficit, not mild global impairment
Test recognition memory as well as free recall, because the distinction between storage and retrieval localises the lesion
Obtain brain MRI: a small thalamic infarct is routinely invisible on CT, as it was during her admission
Exclude the reversible and nutritional causes of an amnestic syndrome
Institute secondary prevention after a documented infarct
Address fitness to practise and driving, since the apathy prevents the patient from raising either
contraindicated_actions: Do not accept a normal head CT as excluding a strategic thalamic infarct
Do not diagnose a degenerative dementia when the deficit began on a datable day and has not progressed in eight months
Do not rely on the patient's own account of her function when apathy and amnesia are both present
Do not conclude 'mild cognitive impairment' from the screen total when one domain accounts for the entire loss
key_reasoning_points: A small lesion in a strategic location produces a dementia out of all proportion to its volume: 0.7 mL in the anterior thalamus interrupts the mamillothalamic tract and with it the Papez circuit

Impaired recognition places the deficit at storage rather than retrieval, and storage-type amnesia localises to the hippocampal-diencephalic circuit — the opposite of the retrieval pattern of small-vessel disease
The screening total is a poor instrument for focal deficits: normal attention, executive function and language with a floor-level recall is a localising pattern, not mild impairment
CT misses small thalamic infarcts routinely, and a normal CT during the index admission is what allowed eight months to pass without a diagnosis

Apathy in a thalamic infarct is part of the lesion syndrome and it removes the patient's own capacity to report the deficit, which makes the informant history and the occupational assessment obligatory

red_herrings.data_point: A MoCA of 23/30, in the mild range
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests mild cognitive impairment not amounting to dementia, and defers the workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The entire loss falls on delayed recall, which is at floor even on recognition, while every other domain is normal or above average; a focal profile at this severity with lost occupational function is a dementia

red_herrings.data_point: A normal head CT during the index admission
red_herrings.intended_effect: Excludes a stroke and supports the discharge diagnosis of a transient confusional state
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Small thalamic infarcts are routinely invisible on CT; the MRI shows the chronic lesion that dates to that admission

key_educational_points: A strategic infarct produces a deficit out of proportion to lesion volume; anterior thalamus, genu of the internal capsule, caudate and angular gyrus are the classic sites
Recognition memory testing separates storage from retrieval deficits and thereby localises the lesion
A normal CT does not exclude a small thalamic infarct
Screening totals conceal focal profiles; the per-domain breakdown is what carries the information

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Single unambiguous strategic lesion with a textbook amnestic profile; the difficulty is only in not being reassured by a MoCA of 23 and a normal CT
